title: Ratios and ratio language
summary: Partners describe a trail-mix recipe with part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios, keep the order of the quantities straight, and extend the recipe in a table of equivalent ratios.

standard.text: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities.

discourse: Explain how two quantities compare by connecting a picture or table to a ratio statement and naming what each number counts (scoops of peanuts, not just 4).
Keep the order of the quantities consistent when restating a ratio, and explain what changes in meaning when the order is reversed (4 to 6 is not 6 to 4).
Describe why a ratio stays the same across the rows of a table: both quantities are multiplied by the same number.
sentence: Ratio statements with a unit noun after each number: For every 2 scoops of peanuts, there are 3 scoops of raisins.
Multiplicative comparisons contrasted with additive ones: there are 3 raisins for every 2 peanuts (ratio) versus there are 2 more raisins than peanuts (difference).
Ratio notation read aloud three ways: 4:6, 4 to 6, and 4/6 all read as four to six in this lesson, not as four sixths.
word: The multiple-meaning word to: direction (walk to the store) versus comparison (4 to 6).
Signal words for a ratio: for every, for each, per, to.
Part-to-part versus part-to-whole: the words total, in all and out of signal that the whole is being named.

contentObjective: Students will describe the relationship between two quantities with part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios and generate equivalent ratios in a table.
languageObjective: Students will explain how two quantities compare using for every ___, there are ___ and ratio notation, naming the unit after each number and keeping the order of the quantities.

L1-2: For every ___ peanuts, there are ___ raisins.
Part-to-part or part-to-whole? It is ___. (Word bank: part, whole, total, to)
L3-4: The ratio of ___ to ___ is ___ to ___ because ___.
For every ___, there are ___, so for ___, there would be ___.
This is a part-to-whole ratio because ___ is the total number of ___.
L5-6: The ratio ___:___ stays the same in every row because both quantities are multiplied by ___.
If we reversed the order to ___ to ___, the statement would mean ___ instead.
Both ratios use the numbers ___ and ___, but one compares ___ and the other compares ___.

vocabulary.definition: a comparison of two quantities, such as 4 scoops of peanuts to 6 scoops of raisins
vocabulary.morphology: from Latin ratio, 'reckoning'; same root as rational

vocabulary.definition: an amount that can be counted or measured
for each group of; used to link the two amounts in a ratio
vocabulary.morphology: two-word phrase; the noun after each number names what is counted

vocabulary.definition: a ratio that compares one part of a group to another part of the same group
vocabulary.morphology: the whole is not mentioned; both numbers are parts

vocabulary.definition: a ratio that compares one part of a group to the whole group
vocabulary.morphology: the second number is the total; listen for in all or out of

vocabulary.definition: ratios that describe the same relationship, such as 4 to 6 and 2 to 3
vocabulary.morphology: equi- 'equal' + val 'worth'; equivalente is a cognate, razón is not

vocabulary.definition: to look at two things to see how they are alike or different

activity.title: Trail Mix Ratio Talk
steps: Write the recipe on the board: one batch of trail mix is 4 scoops of peanuts and 6 scoops of raisins. Draw it on the board as 4 shaded circles (peanuts) and 6 open circles (raisins).

Partner A says one ratio with a frame (For every 4 peanuts, there are 6 raisins). Partner B names it part-to-part or part-to-whole, then says it in reverse order and tells what the new order means. Switch roles twice.
Partners build a table with columns Peanuts and Raisins: 2 and 3, 4 and 6, then fill in 6, 8 and 10 scoops of peanuts. Each partner explains one row aloud using times as many or for every.
Partners solve the problems below. Before writing an answer, each partner says the ratio statement the answer comes from.
Share out: two pairs read one sentence each; the class checks that the quantities are in the stated order and that each number has a unit.

problems.prompt: The recipe uses 4 scoops of peanuts for every 6 scoops of raisins. How many scoops of raisins go with 10 scoops of peanuts?
How many scoops are in one batch in all? Use that total to say the part-to-whole ratio of peanuts to all scoops.
problems.answer: 10 scoops in all, so peanuts to the whole batch is four to ten (or two to five)

problems.prompt: A class has 12 girls and 18 boys. Complete the statement: for every 2 girls, there are ___ boys.

warmup: Project four sentences: I walk to school. The final score was 3 to 2. Give the pencil to Ana. Mix 1 cup of juice to 3 cups of water. Students show one finger if to means direction and two fingers if it compares two amounts. Partners then explain to each other how they knew, and write one new sentence for each meaning.
